turns.text: The previous story examined Neocognitron. Now the camera turns to Convolutional Networks and LeNet and a new question along the same timeline: Turn the clock back to 1989. What problem was Convolutional Networks and LeNet actually trying to solve?
Yann LeCun and collaborators showed that convolutional networks trained by backpropagation could read handwritten ZIP codes. LeNet became a defining example of end-to-end convolutional perception.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?
Convolutions extract local strokes, pooling stabilizes them, and a classifier predicts digits.
Why did the idea outlive one paper or experiment? What did later researchers actually inherit?

Experts generally treat LeNet as a canonical early proof that convolution, weight sharing, and backpropagation could solve real perception tasks. Its long-term legacy is the end-to-end CNN pattern that later scaled into modern computer vision.
Convolutional Networks and LeNet mattered not only as a result, but as a method that later researchers could test, adapt, and extend.
